What are the three main tenses in English?

Tense shows the TIME of an action, and there are three main ones. PRESENT tense describes what happens now or habitually: 'Ada writes a letter.' 'The sun rises in the east.' PAST tense describes what already happened: 'Ada wrote a letter yesterday.' FUTURE tense describes what has not yet happened: 'Ada will write a letter tomorrow.' Each of these has forms that add more detail — for example the present continuous ('Ada is writing') for an action happening at this moment, and the present perfect ('Ada has written') for an action just completed. Time expressions are your clue to the required tense: now, every day and always signal present; yesterday, last week and ago signal past; tomorrow, next month and soon signal future.

What is the difference between simple present and present continuous?

The SIMPLE PRESENT describes habits, routines and general truths — things that happen regularly rather than right now: 'I eat rice every Sunday.' 'Water boils at 100 degrees Celsius.' 'She teaches at our school.' The PRESENT CONTINUOUS describes an action happening at this very moment, and is formed with is/am/are plus a verb ending in -ing: 'I am eating rice now.' 'She is teaching in the next classroom.' Compare carefully: 'Musa plays football' means he plays regularly, perhaps for the school team; 'Musa is playing football' means he is on the pitch at this moment. Time words help you choose: every day, always, usually and often go with simple present, while now, at the moment and look! go with present continuous.

How do I form the past tense of regular and irregular verbs?

REGULAR verbs form the past tense by adding -ed: walk becomes walked, play becomes played, jump becomes jumped. Note the spelling rules: verbs ending in -e just add -d (love becomes loved); verbs ending in a consonant plus -y change y to i and add -ed (study becomes studied, carry becomes carried); and short verbs ending in a single consonant double it (stop becomes stopped, plan becomes planned). IRREGULAR verbs change form completely and must be memorised: go becomes went, eat becomes ate, see becomes saw, take becomes took, write becomes wrote, buy becomes bought, bring becomes brought, teach becomes taught, catch becomes caught. There is no rule for these — the best method is to use five of them in your own sentences each day until they stick.

What is the present perfect tense and when do I use it?

The present perfect is formed with HAS or HAVE plus the past participle: 'She HAS eaten.' 'They HAVE travelled.' Use 'has' with he, she and it, and 'have' with I, you, we and they. You use it in three situations.

First, for an action completed recently, with the result still relevant: 'I have finished my homework' (so it is ready now).
Second, for an action at an unspecified time in the past: 'I have visited Kano before' — we are not saying when.
Third, for something that started in the past and continues: 'She has lived in Enugu for ten years.' Key contrast: 'I ate rice' (simple past) needs a finished time like yesterday, while 'I have eaten rice' focuses on the present result — you are not hungry now. Words like already, just, ever, never, since and for often signal it.

Correct this sentence: Yesterday, Bola go to the market and buy tomatoes.

The correct sentence is: 'Yesterday, Bola WENT to the market and BOUGHT tomatoes.' Here is the reasoning.

Step 1: spot the time word 'Yesterday', which tells us the action is finished, so every verb must be in the past tense.
Step 2: correct each verb. 'Go' is irregular, and its past tense is 'went', not 'goed'. 'Buy' is also irregular, and its past tense is 'bought', not 'buyed'.
Step 3: check consistency — both verbs describe the same past trip, so both must be past; mixing 'went' with 'buy' would be inconsistent. This kind of error is very common in speech, but in writing the examiner expects full agreement between the time word and every verb in the sentence.

What are the different ways of expressing future time in English?

There are three common ways.

First, WILL plus the base verb, for decisions, promises and predictions: 'I will call you tonight.' 'It will rain tomorrow.'
Second, GOING TO plus the base verb, for plans already made or things you can see coming: 'We are going to visit our grandmother next week.' 'Look at those dark clouds — it is going to rain.'
Third, the PRESENT CONTINUOUS for fixed arrangements with a set time: 'I am travelling to Onitsha on Friday.' The simple present can even carry future meaning for timetabled events: 'The bus leaves at 6 a.m. tomorrow.' Note that after 'will', the verb never changes form — say 'She will come', never 'She will comes' or 'She will came'.

Change this sentence to the past continuous tense: The children play in the field.

The past continuous becomes: 'The children WERE PLAYING in the field.' Here is how it is formed: WAS or WERE plus a verb ending in -ing. Use 'was' with singular subjects (I, he, she, it) and 'were' with plural subjects (you, we, they). Since 'children' is plural, we use 'were', and 'play' becomes 'playing'. What does this tense mean? It describes an action that was ongoing at some point in the past, often interrupted by another action: 'The children were playing in the field WHEN the rain started.' Compare the three: 'The children play' (habit), 'The children played' (finished action), 'The children were playing' (action in progress at that past moment). The continuous form paints a picture of the action still happening.

Why do we say 'He goes' but 'They go'?

This is the third-person singular rule of the simple present tense. When the subject is he, she, it, or any singular noun, the verb takes -s or -es. When the subject is I, you, we, they, or any plural noun, the verb stays in its base form. So: 'He GOES to school' but 'They GO to school'; 'She WRITES neatly' but 'We WRITE neatly'; 'The boy PLAYS' but 'The boys PLAY'. Spelling notes: add -es to verbs ending in -s, -sh, -ch, -x or -o (goes, watches, washes, fixes), and change y to ies after a consonant (study becomes studies). Remember the reversal that confuses many students: for NOUNS the -s means plural, but for VERBS the -s means singular. 'The boys play' has the s on the noun; 'The boy plays' has it on the verb.
